source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC1931610 (PLoS One 2007;2(8):e698), read in full in the reader's own browser tab: Abstract, Introduction, Results, Discussion, Materials and Methods, competing interests and funding. No value used by the claim is printed only in a figure; Figures 1-6 were not needed (legends read).

claims.overstatement: None for the part from this source. The claim says 'after a period of escalating cocaine intake', not the authors' 'addicted' rats, and keeps the finding in animals. Nuances the claim could add: (1) the result depends on the alternative being sweet: the same rats preferred cocaine to plain water or to no fluid; (2) cocaine was available only in discrete choice trials 10 minutes apart, about 3 doses a day in all (choices plus sampling) against about 30 that rats take with free access over the same time, so the design does not show what happens with continuous access; (3) the about-16% cocaine choice is an average across experiments (range 7% to 23%), and rats also pressed the cocaine lever 8.3% of the time when it delivered nothing, so not all of it is cocaine seeking; (4) the escalation and intoxication groups were small (11 and 10 rats).
claims.note: All numbers from this source checked against the text: male Wistar rats; 0.25 mg cocaine per intravenous infusion and 20-s access to 0.2% saccharin (study conditions); preference for saccharin significant from day 2 with N = 43; 2.3% (1 of 43, drug-naive), 8.3% (2 of 24, first trained to prefer cocaine) and 0% (0 of 11, after escalation) preferred cocaine, defined as choosing the cocaine lever on more than 60% of trials over the last 3 days; escalation from 7.34 to 26.04 mg/day; cocaine chosen on about 15.6% of choices on average. Degrees of freedom agree with 43 analysed rats in the main choice condition (t(50) for 43 + 9 rats; Condition x Day error df 1106 = 79 x 14 for 30 + 9 + 43 rats). The abstract's 94% preferring saccharin cannot be rebuilt from the 43 (40/43 = 93.0%, 41/43 = 95.3%) and is probably pooled across experiments; the claim's 'almost all' fits both it and the per-group figures. Minor reporting inconsistency, not affecting the claim: the escalation phase is 6 h a day for '3 weeks' in the Results but 18 days in the Methods. 20 of 132 rats (15%) were excluded for completing fewer than half the choice trials, 16 of them in the cocaine-only condition. Rats were housed 2-3 per cage with free food and water and no refined sugar in the diet; this is not a housing study, which the claim marks with 'a different kind of experiment'. The authors' own Discussion goes further than the claim does (sweet diets as a possible shield against drug addiction in people); the claim does not repeat that.

anchors.extracted: 132 young adult male Wistar rats (221-276 g), housed 2-3 per cage on a reversed light cycle, with free food and water in the home cage; standard chow with no synthetic or refined sugar added; tested in the dark phase.

anchors.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Materials and Methods › Discrete-trials choice procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Each day 4 sampling trials (C-S-C-S) then 8 choice trials, 10 min apart, between lever C (one intravenous cocaine dose of 0.25 mg over 4 s) and lever S (20-s access to 0.2% sodium saccharin, at most 0.3 ml). Groups: S-/C+ (only cocaine rewarded) N = 30, S+/C- (only saccharin) N = 9, S+/C+ (both) N = 43.

On day 1 rats in all conditions were indifferent. With both levers rewarded (S+/C+), the preference for saccharin became significant on day 2 and did not differ from that of rats offered saccharin alone (F(14,700) = 0.41, NS); rats offered only cocaine came to prefer the cocaine lever from day 9 (significant on day 11). Latency to choose saccharin 14.5 +/- 5.0 s vs 6.5 +/- 2.4 s in the saccharin-only condition (t(50) < 1).

Rats preferred cocaine over plain water (and over no fluid), so the preference for saccharin was not due to thirst; 4% sucrose gave the same preference as saccharin. Water and no-fluid conditions tested in one group of 10 rats, sucrose in a separate group of 10.

In 11 rats, raising the cocaine dose (0.25 to 1.5 mg, study conditions; highest dose below the convulsive dose) increased locomotion but did not change the preference for saccharin (F(2,20) = 0.07, NS). In 11 rats, delaying saccharin by 0-18 s slightly reduced but did not reverse it; in 10 rats, raising the price from 2 to 8 presses increased it.

anchors.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Materials and Methods › Induction of cocaine intake escalation and › Choice during cocaine intoxication
anchors.extracted: 24 rats that first preferred cocaine (cocaine-only condition) switched to saccharin when both were offered; 8.3% of them vs 2.3% of drug-naive rats still preferred cocaine (more than 60% cocaine choices over the last 3 days; z < 1.96). 11 rats with 6 h a day of cocaine self-administration (3 weeks in the Results, 18 days in the Methods) escalated from 7.34 +/- 2.50 to 26.04 +/- 1.21 mg/day (F(16,160) = 15.98) and then preferred saccharin; 0.0% preferred cocaine. 10 rats given 1 h of cocaine-only access just before the 8 choices (under the influence of cocaine) also quickly came to prefer saccharin.

The preference was not exclusive: rats chose the cocaine lever on about 15.6% of choice trials on average (range across experiments 7% to 23%), about 3 intravenous doses a day with the sampling doses, against about 30 doses rats self-administer freely over the same time. Where the cocaine lever delivered nothing (S+/C-), rats still pressed it 8.3% of the time.

Earlier monkey studies: most monkeys preferred high intravenous cocaine doses over dry food, regardless of the amount of food and despite severe weight loss; the food was mostly not or only lightly sweet, and where lightly sweetened pellets were used the food cost ten times more effort. In one study all monkeys preferred the highest cocaine dose over a 1-g sucrose pellet; the authors cannot exclude a rodent-primate difference.

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods › Data analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 20 of 132 rats excluded for completing fewer than half the daily choice trials after 15 days (16 in the cocaine-only condition, 4 in the both-rewarded condition).

The large majority of rats (94%) preferred saccharin to intravenous cocaine; same preference with sucrose; not overcome by higher cocaine doses, and seen despite cocaine intoxication, sensitization or intake escalation.
